question: Why do parameterized queries ($1, $2) protect against SQL injection, while template strings don't?

options.text: Parameterized queries encrypt values before inserting them into SQL
options.explanation: Values are not encrypted -- they are transmitted separately via the PostgreSQL protocol. The DB receives the SQL template and values separately, so values are never interpreted as SQL code

options.text: Parameters only work with PostgreSQL; other databases need a different approach
options.explanation: Parameterized queries are supported by all SQL databases (MySQL uses ?, SQLite uses ?, MSSQL uses @param). This is the standard defense against SQL injection

options.text: Template strings (${ }) automatically escape quotes
options.explanation: Template strings do NOT escape anything -- they simply substitute the value. If userInput = "'; DROP TABLE users; --", it becomes part of the SQL code

options.text: Parameters are transmitted separately from SQL -- the driver escapes them at the protocol level, not by inserting into the query string

question: Why call client.release() in the finally block after a transaction in pg?

options.text: To return the connection to the pool -- without release(), the connection will leak and the pool will be exhausted
finally is unnecessary -- pg automatically releases connections
options.explanation: pg does NOT automatically release connections on errors. finally guarantees release() even on error, preventing connection pool leaks

options.text: To automatically perform a COMMIT
options.explanation: release() does not perform COMMIT -- you must explicitly call client.query('COMMIT'). release() only returns the connection to the pool. Without COMMIT, the transaction will be rolled back

options.text: To close the connection to PostgreSQL
options.explanation: release() doesn't close the connection -- it returns it to the pool for reuse. Without release(), the connection is considered busy, and new queries wait for a free connection

question: What formula is used to calculate the optimal connection pool size?

options.text: 100 connections by default -- enough for any project
options.explanation: 100 is too many for most projects. Each connection consumes ~10 MB RAM in PostgreSQL. The formula (cores*2)+spindles typically yields 10-20 connections

options.text: Number of concurrent HTTP requests * 2
options.explanation: Tying to HTTP requests is a common mistake. The pool should be small: most requests wait for I/O, not CPU. The formula (cores*2)+spindles is optimal for PostgreSQL

options.text: 1 connection per application user
options.explanation: This would lead to thousands of connections, killing the DB. Connection pools exist precisely so a small number of connections serves many users through multiplexing

options.text: (cpu_cores * 2) + disk_spindles -- on a 4-core CPU with SSD, this is about 10 connections

question: How to prevent deadlocks in parallel transactions?

options.text: Always lock resources in the same order -- sort IDs before SELECT FOR UPDATE
Disable transactions and use individual queries
options.explanation: Without transactions, data may become inconsistent (debited but not credited). Deadlocks are prevented by sorting resources, not by abandoning transactions

options.text: Increase lock_timeout in PostgreSQL
options.explanation: lock_timeout is the wait time for a lock, not deadlock prevention. It prevents hanging forever, but deadlocks will still occur. The solution is lock ordering

options.text: Use READ UNCOMMITTED isolation level
options.explanation: READ UNCOMMITTED doesn't prevent deadlocks -- it reduces isolation, creating other issues (dirty reads). Deadlocks are prevented by lock ordering

options.text: Prisma always generates faster SQL than manual queries
options.explanation: Prisma may generate suboptimal SQL for complex cases. Raw SQL always gives full control. Prisma's advantage is DX and type safety, not performance
